title: The Greek king's questions
hookLine: King Menander, a Greek ruler in India, questions the monk Nagasena (Milinda, Book 2)

lines: A KING WHO WINS EVERY ARGUMENT.
cards: A king rides out of his city with a crowd of courtiers, restless for a debate.

The book that tells his story calls him clever and fond of argument, a man who has questioned teacher after teacher and left each one tongue-tied. Nobody, his courtiers admit, can stand up to him anymore.

Then someone mentions a monk who has just arrived, named Nagasena. The king goes to see him. His name is Milinda in the Pali book, and historians link him with Menander, a Greek ruler in the northwest of India.
The book is called the Questions of King Milinda.

teach.h: SAGALA: A GREEK KING IN INDIA.
teach.b: First, the setting. The book opens in Sagala, a rich city of parks, gates and markets, which it places in the country of the Yonakas, the Greeks.
So the conversation is a meeting of two worlds: a Greek king and a Buddhist monk, talking in India. Second, the ground rules. Early on, the king asks whether Nagasena will keep discussing with him.

teach.h: TALK AS A SCHOLAR, NOT AS A KING.
teach.b: Yes, says Nagasena, if the king talks as a scholar talks; no, if he talks as a king talks. What's the difference? Scholars explain and are explained to, correct and are corrected, and don't get angry about it.
Kings state a view, and whoever disagrees is punished. The king agrees to talk as a scholar. Third, the questions.
They are not polite. Who keeps the precepts, if there is no self? Is the one who is reborn the same person or someone else?
If the Buddha was free of every bad deed, why did he ever feel pain?

teach.h: HARD QUESTIONS, ASKED AT FULL STRENGTH.
teach.b: The king asks what a skeptic would ask, and the book lets him ask it at full strength. Fourth, why this matters. The Theravada tradition kept this book and still teaches from it.

teach.h: A TREASURED BOOK OF AN OUTSIDER'S QUESTIONS.
teach.b: So a text Buddhists value is built out of an outsider's hardest questions, asked in good faith and answered patiently, with the king's doubts in plain view.
Over the next days come Nagasena's answers, one at a time: a chariot, a flame, a stolen mango, a pot of milk.

how: Theravada monks and students read the Questions of King Milinda as a guide to hard questions, and teachers still retell its similes, like the chariot, when explaining the teaching on self.

games.q: you're Nagasena. a powerful king who has silenced every teacher asks if you'll keep talking with him. what do you say?
o: yes, of course. a king must be answered.
yes, if you talk as a scholar talks, not as a king.
no. arguing with kings is dangerous.
games.why: he sets a condition: scholars correct and are corrected without anger; kings punish those who differ. the king agrees to talk as a scholar.

practice: Think of something you honestly don't understand, about this path, about someone in your life, about yourself: not a trap, a real question.
Say it to yourself plainly, the way the king might, and notice how it feels to hold a question without rushing to win it.

wordCard.voice: Milinda. The king of the Questions of King Milinda, linked by historians with the Greek ruler Menander, who asks the monk Nagasena everything.

orig.note: Pali: the king's name in the Milindapanha, the Questions of King Milinda.
